subject: ela
intro: Each item below gives you a written passage and a non-text format (a table, chart, graph, timeline, map, or diagram described in words). The text and the format do not always agree, and their relationship is never spelled out for you. Read both sources carefully, then combine specific details from each to answer the question. For every item, name what the words alone tell you, name what the format alone tells you, and then build one coherent answer from both.

items.prompt:
Passage: The town newsletter praised the new recycling program. It said that ever since the program began in 2018, the town has 'kept more trash out of the landfill every single year.' The writer called the program 'an unbroken success that grows stronger each season.' Residents were told that participation had spread to nearly every neighborhood. The newsletter urged readers to feel proud of steady, year over year improvement.

Table 1: Tons of trash sent to the landfill by year
Year 2018: 4,200 tons
Year 2019: 3,900 tons
Year 2020: 4,050 tons
Year 2021: 3,600 tons
Year 2022: 3,700 tons

Using both the passage and Table 1, explain how the data complicates the newsletter's claim of an 'unbroken' yearly improvement. Identify the specific years that contradict the claim.
items.answer: The newsletter claims trash to the landfill dropped every single year, but Table 1 shows two increases: landfill tonnage rose from 3,900 in 2019 to 4,050 in 2020, and rose again from 3,600 in 2021 to 3,700 in 2022. So while the overall trend from 2018 (4,200) to 2022 (3,700) is downward, the improvement was not 'unbroken,' and the table complicates the newsletter's claim.

steps: From the words alone: the newsletter says the town kept more trash out of the landfill every single year, calling it 'unbroken.'
From Table 1 alone: tonnage went 4,200, 3,900, 4,050, 3,600, 3,700 across 2018 to 2022.
Check each year for a decrease. 2018 to 2019 fell, but 2019 to 2020 rose (3,900 to 4,050), and 2021 to 2022 rose (3,600 to 3,700).
Because landfill tonnage went up in 2020 and again in 2022, the data contradicts the claim that improvement happened every single year.
Combine both: the overall multi-year trend is down, so the program helped, but the table shows the 'unbroken' yearly improvement claim is false in 2020 and 2022.

items.prompt:
Passage: A science article explained that a coral reef off the coast is in trouble. It said the reef 'has been bleaching more and more as the water warms.' The article noted that warmer water stresses coral and can turn it white. It claimed the worst damage came in the warmest years. The author wrote that temperature is 'the single force driving the reef's decline.'

Graph 1: Described line graph titled 'Reef conditions, 2015 to 2020'
Line A (Average water temperature, degrees C): 2015 = 27.0, 2016 = 27.4, 2017 = 27.9, 2018 = 28.3, 2019 = 28.0, 2020 = 28.6
Line B (Percent of reef bleached): 2015 = 10, 2016 = 18, 2017 = 31, 2018 = 45, 2019 = 22, 2020 = 52

The author says temperature is 'the single force' driving bleaching. Using both lines of Graph 1, identify the one year that challenges that claim and explain why.
items.answer: The year 2019 challenges the claim. In 2019 the water temperature dropped slightly (from 28.3 in 2018 to 28.0), and bleaching dropped too (from 45 percent to 22 percent), which fits the author. But the bigger issue is that bleaching did not always rise and fall exactly with temperature: in 2019 temperature was higher than in 2017 (28.0 versus 27.9) yet bleaching was far lower (22 percent versus 31 percent). Combining the graph with the text, temperature clearly matters, but the mismatch in 2019 shows it cannot be the single force, so the data complicates the author's claim.

steps: From the words alone: the author claims temperature is the single force driving the reef's bleaching.
From Graph 1 alone: temperature mostly climbs while bleaching mostly climbs, but read the exact pairs.
Compare 2017 (temp 27.9, bleach 31) with 2019 (temp 28.0, bleach 22). The water was warmer in 2019, yet bleaching was lower.
If temperature were the single force, warmer water should not pair with less bleaching, so 2019 breaks the pattern.
Combine both sources: temperature is a strong factor, but the 2019 data shows another factor must be involved, which complicates the 'single force' claim.

items.prompt:
Passage: A history of a frontier town reported that it boomed after silver was discovered nearby. The text said miners 'poured in by the thousands the moment the first strike was announced.' It described saloons and shops opening within months. The writer claimed the population 'shot up immediately and never looked back.'

Timeline 1: Described timeline of the town
1859: First silver strike announced
1860: Population 800
1862: Population 1,100
1864: Population 5,400
1866: Population 9,200
1868: Population 6,000

Using both the passage and Timeline 1, decide whether the data fully supports the phrase 'shot up immediately and never looked back.' Explain using at least two specific entries.
items.answer: The data only partly supports the phrase. After the 1859 strike, the population in 1860 was just 800 and rose only to 1,100 by 1862, so the growth was slow at first rather than an immediate shot upward; the big jump came later (5,400 in 1864 and 9,200 in 1866). Also, 'never looked back' is contradicted because the population fell from 9,200 in 1866 to 6,000 in 1868. Combining the timeline with the text, the boom was real but delayed and not permanent, so the passage overstates how immediate and lasting the rise was.

steps: From the words alone: the passage claims the population shot up immediately after 1859 and never declined.
Test 'immediately': the first two data points (800, then 1,100) show slow early growth, not an instant surge.
Test 'never looked back': the 1868 figure (6,000) is lower than the 1866 figure (9,200), a clear decline.
Combine both: the timeline shows a delayed boom and a later drop, so it does not fully support the passage's wording.

items.prompt:
Passage: An article about a city's transit system argued that the new express bus line was the fix riders needed. It said the express line 'cut travel time for everyone who switched to it.' The writer insisted that riders on all routes were now reaching downtown faster. The piece called the express line 'a win with no losers.'

Table 2: Average trip time to downtown, in minutes, before and after the express line
Route 1 (local): before 40, after 38
Route 2 (express): before 40, after 25
Route 3 (local): before 35, after 41
Route 4 (express): before 45, after 30

Using both the passage and Table 2, explain how the data both supports and contradicts the claim that the change was 'a win with no losers.' Name the route that contradicts it.
items.answer: The data supports part of the claim because both express routes got much faster (Route 2 went from 40 to 25 minutes and Route 4 from 45 to 30), matching the text's point that express riders saved time. But the claim of 'no losers' is contradicted by Route 3, a local route, whose trip time got worse, rising from 35 to 41 minutes. Combining the table with the passage, the express line helped its own riders but some local riders ended up slower, so it was not a win with no losers.

steps: From the words alone: the article claims the express line was a win with no losers and helped everyone.
From Table 2 alone: Route 2 and Route 4 (express) both dropped a lot, Route 1 dropped slightly, Route 3 rose.
Match the express routes to the text's claim: they support it, since both got faster.
Find the contradiction: Route 3 went from 35 to 41 minutes, meaning those riders got slower, so there was a loser.
Combine both: the table confirms the express benefit but disproves 'no losers' because Route 3 worsened.

items.prompt:
Passage: A nature guide described a bird called the snow finch. It said the finch 'lives only where the air is thin and cold, high in the mountains.' The guide explained that the bird is almost never seen below the tree line. It noted that the finch nests in rocky gaps near the peaks. The author wrote that the bird 'cannot survive in the warmer valleys below.'

Diagram 1: Described elevation diagram of a mountainside, with labeled bands
Band at 600 m: Valley farmland, marked 'finch not recorded'
Band at 1,500 m: Forest, marked 'finch not recorded'
Band at 2,200 m: Upper forest edge, marked 'finch seen rarely'
Band at 2,900 m: Rocky alpine zone, marked 'finch common'
Band at 3,500 m: Peak, marked 'finch common'

Using both the passage and Diagram 1, explain at what elevation the bird first appears and how the diagram both confirms and slightly qualifies the text's claim.
items.answer: The diagram confirms the text's main point because the finch is common only in the high, cold bands at 2,900 m and 3,500 m and is not recorded in the warm valley (600 m) or forest (1,500 m), matching the claim that it lives only high and cold. The diagram qualifies the text slightly because the finch first appears, though only rarely, at 2,200 m at the upper forest edge, which is below the rocky peaks the passage describes. Combining both, the bird is a high-elevation specialist, but the diagram shows its range begins a bit lower than the words suggest.

steps: From the words alone: the finch lives only high and cold and cannot survive in warmer valleys.
From Diagram 1 alone: 'not recorded' at 600 m and 1,500 m, 'seen rarely' at 2,200 m, 'common' at 2,900 m and 3,500 m.
Find the first appearance: the lowest band with any sighting is 2,200 m, the upper forest edge.
Confirm the text: the bird is absent low and common high, supporting the high and cold claim.
Qualify the text: it first shows up at 2,200 m, below the peaks, so the diagram adds that its range starts slightly lower than the words imply.

items.prompt:
Passage: A report on school sports said the swim team had its best season ever. It claimed the team 'won more meets than any year before' and that the swimmers 'improved in every event.' The report praised the new coach for a flawless turnaround. It said the season proved that hard practice 'guarantees a personal best in each race.'

Table 3: Team results across two seasons
Last season meets won: 6 of 10
This season meets won: 8 of 10
Freestyle best time (this season vs last): improved
Backstroke best time: improved
Butterfly best time: slower than last season
Breaststroke best time: improved

Using both the passage and Table 3, identify which part of the report's claim the data contradicts and which part it supports.
items.answer: The data supports the claim that the team won more meets than before, since it won 8 of 10 this season compared with 6 of 10 last season. But the data contradicts the claim that the swimmers 'improved in every event' and got a personal best in each race, because the butterfly best time was slower than last season. Combining the table with the report, the season was strong overall, yet the table disproves the sweeping 'every event' wording.

steps: From the words alone: the report claims more wins than ever and improvement in every event.
From Table 3 alone: wins rose from 6 to 8 of 10; freestyle, backstroke, and breaststroke improved, but butterfly got slower.
Match the wins data to the text: it supports the 'more meets won' claim.
Find the contradiction: butterfly was slower, so not every event improved.
Combine both: the table confirms the record but disproves the 'every event' and 'guarantees a personal best' wording.

items.prompt:
Passage: A travel article about a national park claimed that summer is clearly the best time to visit. It said summer brings 'the most visitors because it offers by far the best weather.' The writer assumed crowds prove a season is best. The article advised readers to avoid other seasons as less pleasant.

Chart 1: Described bar chart titled 'Park visitors and rainy days by season'
Spring: 90,000 visitors, 12 rainy days
Summer: 210,000 visitors, 9 rainy days
Fall: 120,000 visitors, 5 rainy days
Winter: 40,000 visitors, 15 rainy days

Using both the passage and Chart 1, explain how the data complicates the article's reasoning that the busiest season must have the best weather.
items.answer: The chart shows summer is indeed the busiest season with 210,000 visitors, which the article uses as proof of the best weather. But the rainy-day data complicates that reasoning: fall has the fewest rainy days at only 5, fewer than summer's 9, even though fall has far fewer visitors (120,000). So if 'best weather' means the driest, fall, not summer, would win. Combining the chart with the text, crowd size does not prove best weather, so the article's reasoning is weak.

steps: From the words alone: the article assumes the busiest season (summer) must have the best weather.
From Chart 1 alone: summer has the most visitors (210,000) but 9 rainy days, while fall has 5 rainy days.
Compare the weather measure: fall has fewer rainy days than summer, so summer is not the driest.
This breaks the article's logic, because the busiest season does not have the fewest rainy days.
Combine both: the chart shows visitor numbers and weather quality do not line up, complicating the claim.

items.prompt:
Passage: An article about electric cars stated that they are spreading fast. It said that in one state, 'sales have climbed steadily and now dominate the road.' The writer claimed electric cars made up most new vehicles sold and were close to outnumbering gas cars overall. The piece said the shift was 'nearly complete.'

Table 4: New car sales in the state, by type
Year 2020 electric: 5 percent of new sales
Year 2022 electric: 12 percent of new sales
Year 2024 electric: 22 percent of new sales
Share of ALL cars on the road that are electric, 2024: 6 percent

Using both the passage and Table 4, explain how the data corrects the article's claim that electric cars 'dominate the road' and the shift is 'nearly complete.'
items.answer: The table confirms that electric sales are climbing steadily, from 5 percent in 2020 to 12 percent in 2022 to 22 percent in 2024, which supports the 'climbed steadily' part. But it corrects the article's bigger claim: electric cars are still only 22 percent of new sales, not most, and only 6 percent of all cars on the road, so they do not dominate the road and the shift is far from nearly complete. Combining the table with the text, the trend is rising but the passage overstates how far the change has gone.

steps: From the words alone: the article claims electric cars dominate the road and the shift is nearly complete.
From Table 4 alone: electric is 22 percent of new sales in 2024 and only 6 percent of all cars on the road.
Test 'dominate the road': 6 percent of all cars is a small share, not domination.
Test 'nearly complete': 22 percent of new sales means most new cars are still not electric.
Combine both: the data supports a rising trend but corrects the exaggerated claims of domination and near completion.

items.prompt:
Passage: A field report on a wolf pack said the pack was thriving. It claimed the wolves 'grew their numbers every year as prey became more plentiful.' The report tied wolf survival directly to the deer population. It stated that 'whenever deer are up, the wolves are up, without exception.'

Graph 2: Described double line graph titled 'Wolves and deer, 2016 to 2021'
Deer (hundreds): 2016 = 20, 2017 = 24, 2018 = 30, 2019 = 28, 2020 = 33, 2021 = 31
Wolves: 2016 = 8, 2017 = 9, 2018 = 11, 2019 = 12, 2020 = 11, 2021 = 13

Using both the passage and Graph 2, find the year that breaks the rule 'whenever deer are up, the wolves are up, without exception' and explain.
items.answer: The year 2019 breaks the rule. From 2018 to 2019 the deer population went down (from 30 to 28 hundred), yet the wolves went up (from 11 to 12). The report says wolves rise only when deer rise, but here wolves rose while deer fell. A second break is 2020, when deer rose (28 to 33) but wolves fell (12 to 11). Combining the graph with the text, the two populations are loosely linked but the data disproves the 'without exception' claim.

steps: From the words alone: the report claims wolves go up only when deer go up, without exception.
From Graph 2 alone: list the year-to-year changes for both lines.
From 2018 to 2019, deer dropped (30 to 28) but wolves rose (11 to 12), which violates the rule.
From 2019 to 2020, deer rose (28 to 33) but wolves dropped (12 to 11), a second violation.
Combine both: the graph shows exceptions, so the text's 'without exception' claim is false.

items.prompt:
Passage: A community blog praised a new downtown plaza. It said the plaza 'made the area safer and busier at all hours.' The writer claimed foot traffic rose around the clock after the plaza opened. The post insisted that 'every part of the day saw more visitors than before.'

Table 5: Average people counted downtown per hour, before and after the plaza opened
Morning (6 to 10 a.m.): before 120, after 150
Midday (10 a.m. to 2 p.m.): before 300, after 360
Evening (5 to 9 p.m.): before 250, after 410
Late night (10 p.m. to 2 a.m.): before 60, after 45

Using both the passage and Table 5, decide whether the data supports the claim that 'every part of the day' saw more visitors. Name the time block that contradicts it.
items.answer: The data supports the claim for most of the day: morning rose from 120 to 150, midday from 300 to 360, and evening from 250 to 410, all increases. But the claim that 'every part of the day' saw more visitors is contradicted by the late-night block, which fell from 60 to 45 people per hour. Combining the table with the passage, the plaza did boost daytime and evening traffic, yet the data disproves the sweeping 'all hours' claim.

steps: From the words alone: the blog claims every part of the day got busier after the plaza opened.
From Table 5 alone: morning, midday, and evening all rose, but late night fell.
Match the rising blocks to the text: they support most of the claim.
Find the contradiction: late night dropped from 60 to 45, so not every part of the day rose.
Combine both: the table confirms a daytime boost but disproves the 'all hours' and 'every part of the day' wording.

items.prompt:
Passage: A report on a river cleanup said the water kept getting cleaner. It explained that scientists measure cleanliness two ways: a higher oxygen level is better, and a lower bacteria count is better. The report claimed that 'by both measures, the river improved each year.' It credited new sewage rules for the steady gains.

Table 6: River readings by year (oxygen in mg per liter, bacteria in colonies per 100 mL)
Year 2019: oxygen 5.0, bacteria 900
Year 2020: oxygen 5.6, bacteria 720
Year 2021: oxygen 6.1, bacteria 800
Year 2022: oxygen 6.4, bacteria 540

Using both the passage and Table 6, explain how the data partly contradicts the claim that the river improved by both measures every year.
items.answer: Oxygen rose every year (5.0, 5.6, 6.1, 6.4), so by that measure the river improved each year, supporting the report. But bacteria did not fall every year: it dropped from 900 to 720 in 2020, then rose to 800 in 2021 before falling to 540 in 2022. Since a lower bacteria count is better, the 2021 rise means the river got worse by the bacteria measure that year. Combining the table with the text, the river improved overall, but the claim that it improved by both measures every single year is contradicted in 2021.

steps: From the words alone: the report claims improvement by both measures (oxygen up, bacteria down) every year.
From Table 6 alone: oxygen is 5.0, 5.6, 6.1, 6.4; bacteria is 900, 720, 800, 540.
Check oxygen: it rises every year, so that measure supports the claim.
Check bacteria: it falls, then rises to 800 in 2021, which is worse since lower is better.
Combine both: the 2021 bacteria rise contradicts the 'both measures every year' claim even though oxygen always improved.

items.prompt:
Passage: A magazine article said a famous explorer's route went smoothly from start to finish. It described the explorer sailing west, landing on an island, then continuing west to the mainland in one steady push. The writer said the journey 'moved in a single direction without backtracking.' The article praised the explorer's straight, efficient path.

Map 1: Described map with labeled points and a dashed route line
Point A: Home port (east side of map)
Point B: Storm Island (middle of map)
Point C: Rocky Cape (far west of map)
Point D: Mainland Harbor (west of center, east of Rocky Cape)
Route order along the dashed line: A, then B, then C, then back east to D

Using both the passage and Map 1, explain how the map contradicts the claim that the journey moved in a single direction without backtracking.
items.answer: The passage says the explorer moved steadily west without backtracking, but Map 1 shows the route went A to B to C and then back east to D, since Mainland Harbor (D) lies east of Rocky Cape (C). Sailing from C back east to D is a reversal of direction, which is exactly the backtracking the text denies. Combining the map with the passage, the journey did head west at first, but the map proves it doubled back, contradicting the 'single direction without backtracking' claim.

steps: From the words alone: the article claims the route went one direction (west) with no backtracking.
From Map 1 alone: the route order is A, B, C, then D, and D is east of C.
Find the direction change: going from C (far west) to D (east of C) means heading back east.
That eastward leg is backtracking, which the text says did not happen.
Combine both: the map's route order disproves the 'single direction without backtracking' claim.

items.prompt:
Passage: A health article argued that a town's new bike lanes had made cycling far safer. It said that since the lanes opened, 'crashes involving bikes have dropped sharply.' The writer credited the lanes alone for the drop. The article also mentioned, almost in passing, that far fewer people were biking now because a popular bike shop had closed.

Table 7: Bike data in the town, before and after the lanes
Reported bike crashes per year: before 80, after 50
Number of regular bike riders: before 4,000, after 2,000

Using both the passage and Table 7, explain why the drop in crashes might not prove the lanes made cycling safer. Combine the text detail about ridership with the table.
items.answer: Crashes did drop from 80 to 50, which the article credits to the lanes. But Table 7 shows the number of regular riders also fell sharply, from 4,000 to 2,000, and the passage itself mentions fewer people are biking after a bike shop closed. With half as many riders, fewer crashes could be expected even if biking were no safer per rider. In fact, 80 crashes among 4,000 riders is 1 crash per 50 riders, while 50 crashes among 2,000 riders is 1 per 40 riders, slightly worse per rider. Combining the text and table, the raw drop in crashes does not prove the lanes made cycling safer.

steps: From the words alone: the article credits the lanes for a sharp drop in crashes, but it also notes fewer people are biking.
From Table 7 alone: crashes fell from 80 to 50, and riders fell from 4,000 to 2,000.
Connect the text detail to the data: with half as many riders, fewer total crashes is expected even without added safety.
Compare crashes per rider: before is 80 of 4,000 (1 per 50), after is 50 of 2,000 (1 per 40), which is not safer per rider.
Combine both: the raw crash drop does not prove the lanes worked, because ridership dropped too.

items.prompt:
Passage: An article on three nearby towns claimed they were all growing in the same way. It said each town 'gained people steadily as new factories opened.' The writer treated the three towns as identical success stories. The piece concluded that the whole region was 'rising together, town by town.'

Table 8: Population change in three towns, 2015 to 2023
Riverton: 2015 = 12,000, 2023 = 16,000
Millbrook: 2015 = 9,000, 2023 = 9,200
Oakdale: 2015 = 14,000, 2023 = 11,500

Using both the passage and Table 8, explain how the data challenges the claim that the three towns grew 'together' in the same way. Refer to each town.
items.answer: The data challenges the claim because the three towns did not change the same way. Riverton grew strongly, from 12,000 to 16,000, which fits the article. But Millbrook barely changed, rising only from 9,000 to 9,200, which is close to flat rather than steady growth. Oakdale actually shrank, from 14,000 to 11,500. Combining the table with the text, only one town clearly grew, so the claim that all three rose 'together, town by town' is contradicted by Millbrook's near-flat numbers and Oakdale's decline.

steps: From the words alone: the article claims all three towns grew steadily and rose together.
From Table 8 alone: Riverton 12,000 to 16,000, Millbrook 9,000 to 9,200, Oakdale 14,000 to 11,500.
Check each town: Riverton clearly grew, Millbrook stayed nearly flat, Oakdale lost population.
Since one town grew, one was flat, and one shrank, they did not change in the same way.
Combine both: the table shows uneven results, contradicting the 'rising together, town by town' claim.

items.prompt:
Passage: A report praised a study program for raising test scores. It said students in the program 'scored higher on the final exam than students who were not in it.' The report concluded that the program clearly caused the higher scores. It noted, however, that the program only accepted students who had already passed an entry quiz with high marks.

Table 9: Average final exam score and average entry quiz score by group
Program students: entry quiz 88, final exam 91
Non-program students: entry quiz 70, final exam 78

Using both the passage and Table 9, explain why the higher final scores may not prove the program caused them. Combine the text detail about the entry quiz with the table.
items.answer: Program students did score higher on the final, 91 versus 78, which the report credits to the program. But Table 9 shows the two groups were not equal to begin with: program students entered with an average quiz score of 88, far above the non-program students' 70, and the passage says the program only accepted high scorers. The program students were already stronger before the program started. Combining the text and table, their higher final scores may come from their head start, not from the program, so the data weakens the claim that the program caused the gain.

steps: From the words alone: the report claims the program caused the higher final scores, and it admits only high quiz scorers were accepted.
From Table 9 alone: program students scored entry 88 and final 91; non-program students scored entry 70 and final 78.
Connect the text detail to the data: the program group started far ahead on the entry quiz (88 versus 70).
Because the groups were unequal before the program, the final gap could reflect that head start, not the program.
Combine both: the entry-quiz gap shown in the table undercuts the claim that the program caused the higher scores.
